claim: Activation/deactivation of specific brain regions has been shown to be predictive of successful memory encoding.
source: Although activation/deactivation of specific brain regions has been shown to be predictive of successful memory encoding, the relationship between time-varying large-scale brain networks and fluctuations of memory encoding performance remains unclear.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research in the field.

claim: The relationship between time-varying large-scale brain networks and fluctuations of memory encoding performance remains unclear.
source: Although activation/deactivation of specific brain regions has been shown to be predictive of successful memory encoding, the relationship between time-varying large-scale brain networks and fluctuations of memory encoding performance remains unclear.
evidence: This is a statement about the current state of knowledge in the field.

claim: Increased integration of the subcortical, default-mode, salience, and visual subnetworks with other subnetworks is a hallmark of successful memory encoding.
source: A graph analysis of functional connectivity patterns revealed that increased integration of the subcortical, default-mode, salience, and visual subnetworks with other subnetworks is a hallmark of successful memory encoding.
evidence: This claim is based on graph analysis results presented in the study.

claim: Multivariate analysis using the graph metrics of integration reliably classified the brain network states into the period of high (vs. low) memory encoding performance.
source: Moreover, multivariate analysis using the graph metrics of integration reliably classified the brain network states into the period of high (vs. low) memory encoding performance.
evidence: This claim is supported by multivariate classification analysis results.

claim: A diverse set of brain systems dynamically interact to support successful memory encoding.
source: Our findings suggest that a diverse set of brain systems dynamically interact to support successful memory encoding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: Regions such as the medial temporal lobes (MTL) and the prefrontal cortex show greater activation in response to stimuli successfully recalled later (vs. forgotten).
source: Studies using functional magnetic resonance imaging (fMRI) have demonstrated that regions such as the medial temporal lobes (MTL) and the prefrontal cortex show greater activation in response to stimuli successfully recalled later (vs. forgotten), a phenomenon referred to as the subsequent memory effect (SME) (Wagner et al., 1998; Brewer et al., 1998; Paller and Wagner, 2002; Reber et al., 2002; Uncapher and Rugg, 2005; Kim, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple previous fMRI studies.

claim: Brain regions such as the posterior cingulate cortex and temporoparietal junction tend to show stronger activation (or weaker deactivation) in response to stimuli that are later forgotten (vs. remembered).
source: On the other hand, brain regions such as the posterior cingulate cortex and temporoparietal junction tend to show stronger activation (or weaker deactivation) in response to stimuli that are later forgotten (vs. remembered), referred to as the subsequent forgetting effect (SFE) (Wagner and Davachi, 2001; Otten and Rugg, 2001; Daselaar et al., 2004; Kim, 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous research.

claim: Successful memory encoding is related to enhanced functional connectivity (FC) between memory-related regions.
source: In addition, several studies have shown that successful memory encoding is related to enhanced functional connectivity (FC) between memory-related regions (Ranganath et al., 2005; Summerfield et al., 2006; Schott et al., 2013; Liu et al., 2014), such as between the hippocampus and other areas.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Memory encoding is thought to require orchestration among many brain systems beyond the so-called memory system.
source: However, memory encoding is thought to require orchestration among many brain systems beyond the so-called memory system, because encoding success depends on a range of factors (e.g., attention, arousal, and motivation) processed in distributed brain networks (Chun and Turk-Browne, 2007; Gruber et al., 2014; Tambini et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents current understanding in the field.

claim: Large-scale brain networks dynamically fluctuate, typically within a timescale of 30–40 s.
source: Notably, recent studies have revealed that large-scale brain networks dynamically fluctuate, typically within a timescale of 30–40 s (Mohr et al., 2016; Wang et al., 2016; Braun et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent studies.

claim: Dynamic fluctuations of large-scale FC patterns are associated with a variety of cognitive processes.
source: Furthermore, these studies have shown that dynamic fluctuations of large-scale FC patterns are associated with a variety of cognitive processes (Bassett et al., 2011; Cole et al., 2014; Bassett et al., 2015; Sadaghiani et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016; Mohr et al., 2016; Cohen, 2017; Kucyi et al., 2018), and even exist during the resting state (Zalesky et al., 2014; Calhoun et al., 2014; Allen et al., 2014; Betzel et al., 2016; Shine et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: Integration of large-scale networks is important for efficient communication across entire systems.
source: Theoretically, integration of large-scale networks is important for efficient communication across entire systems, whereas segregation is critical for specialized functioning of particular modules without interference from the rest of the network (Bassett et al., 2013; Bassett et al., 2015; Sadaghiani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents theoretical understanding.

claim: Segregation is critical for specialized functioning of particular modules without interference from the rest of the network.
source: Theoretically, integration of large-scale networks is important for efficient communication across entire systems, whereas segregation is critical for specialized functioning of particular modules without interference from the rest of the network (Bassett et al., 2013; Bassett et al., 2015; Sadaghiani et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations and represents theoretical understanding.

claim: The degrees of integration and segregation in the brain dynamically change over time.
source: Accumulating evidence suggests that the degrees of integration and segregation in the brain dynamically change over time (Deco et al., 2015; Cohen and D'Esposito, 2016; Shine et al., 2016; Lord et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to multiple studies.

claim: When the brain processes a cognitively demanding task, the degree of integration tends to increase.
source: For example, when the brain processes a cognitively demanding task (e.g., the N-back working memory task), the degree of integration tends to increase, which is suitable for efficient communication among the sensory, motor and cognitive control systems.
evidence: This claim is based on previous research findings.

claim: The degree of segregation tends to increase over time as the brain learns specialized skills.
source: On the other hand, the degree of segregation tends to increase over time as the brain learns specialized skills, which allows automatic processing of a habitual task without effortful cognitive control (Bassett et al., 2015; Mohr et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous studies.

claim: Participants were able to correctly distinguish between studied and unstudied pictures with accuracy of 74.2 ± 6.3%.
source: Although participants were not informed about the surprise memory test after the fMRI scan, they were able to correctly distinguish between studied and unstudied pictures with accuracy of 74.2 ± 6.3% (mean ± SD across participants).
evidence: This claim is based on behavioral data collected in the study.

claim: 67.7 ± 15.9% of the studied pictures were judged as studied (i.e., hit).
source: 67.7 ± 15.9% of the studied pictures were judged as studied (i.e., hit), whereas 80.8 ± 14.6% of the unstudied pictures were judged as unstudied (i.e., correct rejection).
evidence: This claim is based on behavioral data from the study.

claim: 80.8 ± 14.6% of the unstudied pictures were judged as unstudied (i.e., correct rejection).
source: 67.7 ± 15.9% of the studied pictures were judged as studied (i.e., hit), whereas 80.8 ± 14.6% of the unstudied pictures were judged as unstudied (i.e., correct rejection).
evidence: This claim is based on behavioral data from the study.

claim: The number of windows classified as the high encoding state (22.7 ± 1.9) and the low encoding state (22.3 ± 1.9) were closely matched.
source: We confirmed that the number of windows classified as the high encoding state (22.7 ± 1.9, mean ± SD across participants) and the low encoding state (22.3 ± 1.9) were closely matched (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, z24)=1.0968, p=0.2727).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of the window classification.

claim: The proportion of HH trials was 64.6 ± 15.4% for the high encoding state and 32.6 ± 15.0% for the low encoding state.
source: The proportion of HH trials was 64.6 ± 15.4% (5.18 ± 1.25 trials per window) for the high encoding state and 32.6 ± 15.0% (2.59 ± 1.17 trials per window) for the low encoding state, confirming a difference in encoding performance between the two states.
evidence: This claim is based on data analysis of trial proportions.

claim: The proportion of the high encoding state was close to 50% in all three sessions.
source: It should be noted that the proportion of the high encoding state was close to 50% in all three sessions (session 1: 51.2 ± 19.7%, session 2: 45.9 ± 18.7%, session 3: 54.1 ± 13.2%, mean ± SD across participants), with no increasing or decreasing trend over time (F(2,24) = 1.020, p=0.367, one-way ANOVA).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical analysis of session data.

claim: Window-wise encoding performance is not influenced by a mere effect of temporal proximity to the surprise memory test.
source: It should be noted that the proportion of the high encoding state was close to 50% in all three sessions (session 1: 51.2 ± 19.7%, session 2: 45.9 ± 18.7%, session 3: 54.1 ± 13.2%, mean ± SD across participants), with no increasing or decreasing trend over time (F(2,24) = 1.020, p=0.367, one-way ANOVA). This ruled out the possibility that window-wise encoding performance is influenced by a mere effect of temporal proximity to the surprise memory test.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the lack of temporal trend in the data.

claim: The probability of state switching was significantly lower than the theoretical chance level of 50%.
source: However, we found that the probability was significantly lower than the theoretical chance level of 50% (41.0%, p<0.001, permutation test).
evidence: This claim is based on permutation test results.

claim: The state type of a window tended to be carried over to the next window.
source: This indicated a history dependence of window-wide encoding performance, such that the state type of a window tended to be carried over to the next window.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the state switching probability results.

claim: Trial-related activation analysis confirmed the SME and SFE in the ROIs.
source: Importantly, trial-related activation analysis of our own fMRI data confirmed the SME and SFE in these ROIs (Figure 3A–C; Supplementary file 1B).
evidence: This claim is based on activation analysis results shown in Figure 3.

claim: FC increases during the high vs. low encoding state were observed between some pairs of SME-related ROIs, most notably in the right middle occipital gyrus (MOG)-right hippocampus/parahippocampal gyrus (HCP/PHG) pair.
source: While the connectivity matrices of the two states appeared to be similar, direct comparison revealed a trend indicating FC increases during the high vs. low encoding state between some pairs of SME-related ROIs, most notably in the right middle occipital gyrus (MOG)-right hippocampus/parahippocampal gyrus (HCP/PHG) pair, the right MOG-left fusiform gyrus pair, and the left inferior occipital gyrus-left HCP/PHG pair (Wilcoxon signed-rank test, z(24) = 2.3274–3.0808, p=0.0021–0.0199; Figure 3F).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical comparison of connectivity matrices shown in Figure 3F.

claim: The FC increases between SME-related ROI pairs did not survive false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction.
source: However, it should be noted that these results did not survive false-discovery-rate (FDR) correction among 21C2 = 210 tests.
evidence: This is a statement about the statistical significance after correction.

claim: Neither the within-subnetwork connectivity for the SME regions nor that for the SFE regions showed a significant difference between the high and low encoding states.
source: Neither the within-subnetwork connectivity for the SME regions nor that for the SFE regions showed a significant difference between the high and low encoding states (Wilcoxon signed-rank test; SME: z(24) = 0.4709, p=0.6377; SFE: z(24) = 0.6592, p=0.5098; Figure 3G).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical tests of within-subnetwork connectivity.

claim: 98 connections showed significant increases in FC during the high encoding states.
source: By comparing the high and low encoding states, we found significant differences in FC associated with encoding performance: 98 connections showed significant increases in FC during the high encoding states, whereas 687 connections showed significant decreases (surviving FDR corrections among 224C2 = 24,976 tests; Figure 4C; Supplementary file 1D and 1E).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical comparison of FC patterns shown in Figure 4C.

claim: 687 connections showed significant decreases in FC during the high encoding states.
source: By comparing the high and low encoding states, we found significant differences in FC associated with encoding performance: 98 connections showed significant increases in FC during the high encoding states, whereas 687 connections showed significant decreases (surviving FDR corrections among 224C2 = 24,976 tests; Figure 4C; Supplementary file 1D and 1E).
evidence: This claim is based on statistical comparison of FC patterns shown in Figure 4C.

claim: The connections showing significant increases in FC during the high encoding state tended to be long range (Euclidean distance: 84.6 ± 27.3).
source: Interestingly, the connections showing significant increases in FC during the high encoding state tended to be long range (Euclidean distance: 84.6 ± 27.3; Figure 4D), whereas those showing significant decreases tended to be short range (Euclidean distance: 76.5 ± 29.7; Figure 4E; increases vs. decreases: z(783) = 2.7846, p<0.0054, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of Euclidean distances of connections.

claim: The connections showing significant decreases in FC during the high encoding state tended to be short range (Euclidean distance: 76.5 ± 29.7).
source: Interestingly, the connections showing significant increases in FC during the high encoding state tended to be long range (Euclidean distance: 84.6 ± 27.3; Figure 4D), whereas those showing significant decreases tended to be short range (Euclidean distance: 76.5 ± 29.7; Figure 4E; increases vs. decreases: z(783) = 2.7846, p<0.0054, Wilcoxon rank-sum test).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of Euclidean distances of connections.

claim: There is a systematic reconfiguration of the large-scale network between the high and low encoding states.
source: These observations suggest a systematic reconfiguration of the large-scale network between the high and low encoding states, rather than a homogeneous, brain-wide increase or decrease in FC.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FC pattern differences.

claim: Increased FC was observed between the hippocampus and occipital cortex during the high vs. low encoding state.
source: As expected, we observed increased FC between the hippocampus and occipital cortex during the high vs. low encoding state (right hippocampus-left MOG: z(24) = 3.5383, p<0.004; surviving FDR corrections among 226C2 = 25,425 tests; Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on FC analysis including the hippocampus.

claim: Global efficiency was significantly higher during the high (vs. low) encoding state.
source: We found that global efficiency was significantly higher during the high (vs. low) encoding state (z(24) = 3.9688, p=0.0001; Figure 5A), whereas local efficiency was not different between the states (z(24) = 0.6861, p=0.4926; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on graph analysis results shown in Figure 5A.

claim: Local efficiency was not different between the high and low encoding states.
source: We found that global efficiency was significantly higher during the high (vs. low) encoding state (z(24) = 3.9688, p=0.0001; Figure 5A), whereas local efficiency was not different between the states (z(24) = 0.6861, p=0.4926; Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is based on graph analysis results shown in Figure 5C.

claim: A two-way ANOVA showed a significant interaction between state (high vs. low) and metrics (global vs. local efficiency).
source: A two-way ANOVA showed a significant interaction (F(1,24) = 17.1006, p=0.0004) between state (high vs. low) and metrics (global vs. local efficiency), confirming that only the measure of integration changed in association with memory encoding performance.
evidence: This claim is based on ANOVA results.

claim: Only the measure of integration changed in association with memory encoding performance.
source: A two-way ANOVA showed a significant interaction (F(1,24) = 17.1006, p=0.0004) between state (high vs. low) and metrics (global vs. local efficiency), confirming that only the measure of integration changed in association with memory encoding performance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the ANOVA interaction result.

claim: The salience network showed significantly higher participation coefficients during the high (vs. low) encoding state.
source: When we examined individual subnetworks, we found significantly higher PCs during the high (vs. low) encoding state in two subnetworks (salience network [SAN]: z(24) = 3.0001, p=0.0027; subcortical nodes [SUB]: z(24) = 3.7535, p=0.0002; surviving FDR correction among 10 tests; Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on subnetwork-wise PC analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: The subcortical nodes showed significantly higher participation coefficients during the high (vs. low) encoding state.
source: When we examined individual subnetworks, we found significantly higher PCs during the high (vs. low) encoding state in two subnetworks (salience network [SAN]: z(24) = 3.0001, p=0.0027; subcortical nodes [SUB]: z(24) = 3.7535, p=0.0002; surviving FDR correction among 10 tests; Figure 5B).
evidence: This claim is based on subnetwork-wise PC analysis shown in Figure 5B.

claim: Only the SAN showed a significant state-by-metric interaction.
source: We found a significant state-by-metric interaction only in the SAN (F(1,24) = 11.9399, p=0.0021; surviving FDR correction among 10 tests). This result confirmed that only the subnetwork-wise integration, not segregation, was associated with memory encoding performance in the SAN.
evidence: This claim is based on ANOVA results for individual subnetworks.

claim: Only the subnetwork-wise integration, not segregation, was associated with memory encoding performance in the SAN.
source: We found a significant state-by-metric interaction only in the SAN (F(1,24) = 11.9399, p=0.0021; surviving FDR correction among 10 tests). This result confirmed that only the subnetwork-wise integration, not segregation, was associated with memory encoding performance in the SAN.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the state-by-metric interaction result.

claim: Higher inter-subnetwork efficiency for the high encoding state was observed among some subnetworks, e.g., between the SUB, SAN, DMN, and VIN and the rest of the subnetworks.
source: Specifically, higher inter-subnetwork efficiency for the high encoding state was observed among some subnetworks, e.g., between the SUB, SAN, DMN, and VIN and the rest of the subnetworks (z(24) > 2.3274, p<0.0199).
evidence: This claim is based on inter-subnetwork efficiency analysis.

claim: Only the SMN-AUD pair showed lower inter-subnetwork efficiency for the high encoding state.
source: Only the SMN-AUD pair showed lower inter-subnetwork efficiency for the high encoding state (z(24) = −2.7041, p=0.0068).
evidence: This claim is based on inter-subnetwork efficiency analysis.

claim: Modularity was significantly higher during the high encoding state.
source: We also examined modularity, a measure of entire network-level segregation indicating how well a network can be partitioned into distinct communities (Westphal et al., 2017; Wig, 2017). Unlike the results for local efficiency, we observed significantly higher modularity during the high encoding state (z(24) = 2.5427, p=0.0110).
evidence: This claim is based on modularity analysis results.

claim: There was no significant correlation between modularity and global efficiency on a window-to-window basis.
source: To clarify the relationship between modularity and global efficiency, we computed a window-to-window correlation (within each individual) between the two metrics. We found no significant correlation between the two metrics (Pearson's r = 0.1155 ± 0.4408; z(24) = 1.3319, p=0.1829), suggesting that these two graph metrics captured somewhat independent aspects of the network architecture.
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis.

claim: There was a positive correlation between modularity and entire-network local efficiency on a window-to-window basis.
source: We also computed a window-to-window correlation between modularity and entire-network local efficiency, revealing a positive correlation (Pearson's r = 0.5907 ± 0.1525; z(24) = 4.3724, p=1.2290 × 10−5), consistent with the notion that both modularity and local efficiency are metrics of segregation.
evidence: This claim is based on correlation analysis.

claim: Both the proportion of edges within the SUB and those across the SUB and the other subnetworks increased during the high encoding state.
source: We found that both the proportion of edges within the SUB and those across the SUB and the other subnetworks increased during the high encoding state (within: z(24) = 3.0003, p=0.0027; across: z(24) = 2.7580, p=0.0058).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of edge proportions.

claim: The increase in the proportion of edges (high vs. low encoding states) was greater for the connections within the SUB than those across the SUB and the other subnetworks.
source: In addition, the increase in the proportion of edges (high vs. low encoding states) was greater for the connections within the SUB than those across the SUB and the other subnetworks (z(24) = 2.5965, p=0.0094), in line with the increased modularity contribution observed in the SUB.
evidence: This claim is based on statistical comparison of edge proportion increases.

claim: The SUB contributed to entire network-level segregation by its increased within-subnetwork connections.
source: These findings suggest that the SUB contributed to entire network-level segregation (i.e., modularity) by its increased within-subnetwork connections, and also contributed to inter-subnetwork integration by its increased connection with other subnetworks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the edge proportion analysis results.

claim: The SUB contributed to inter-subnetwork integration by its increased connection with other subnetworks.
source: These findings suggest that the SUB contributed to entire network-level segregation (i.e., modularity) by its increased within-subnetwork connections, and also contributed to inter-subnetwork integration by its increased connection with other subnetworks.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the edge proportion analysis results.

claim: The DMN was divided into five submodules.
source: By applying a group-level modular decomposition method (Fornito et al., 2012), we found that the DMN (consisting of 56 nodes) was divided into five submodules (Figure 7; Supplementary file 1G).
evidence: This claim is based on modular decomposition analysis shown in Figure 7.

claim: The submodule assignment of the DMN nodes was identical between the high and low encoding states.
source: Importantly, the submodule assignment of the DMN nodes was identical between the high and low encoding states, suggesting that the DMN submodule structure did not change between the two states.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of submodule assignments.

claim: Using subnetwork-wise PCs as input, SVM classification distinguished the high from low encoding states with 74% accuracy.
source: When we used the subnetwork-wise PCs (i.e., 10 features) as the input of the SVM classifier, we were able to reliably distinguish the high from low encoding states with 74% classification accuracy (p=0.0094, permutation test; Figure 8A).
evidence: This claim is based on SVM classification results shown in Figure 8A.

claim: Using subnetwork-wise local efficiency as input, SVM classification obtained 68% accuracy.
source: Likewise, when we used subnetwork-wise local efficiency, we obtained a classification accuracy of 68% (p=0.0267, permutation test; Figure 8B).
evidence: This claim is based on SVM classification results shown in Figure 8B.

claim: Using inter-subnetwork efficiency as input, SVM classification obtained 72% accuracy.
source: Using inter-subnetwork efficiency (i.e., 45 features) as inputs, we obtained a classification accuracy of 72% (p=0.0029, permutation test; Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is based on SVM classification results shown in Figure 8C.

claim: When using the entire FC patterns as input, SVM classification accuracy dropped to chance levels (36%).
source: Notably, when we used the entire FC patterns (i.e., Fisher Z-transform of Pearson's correlation coefficients, 224C2 = 24,976 features) as the input, classification accuracy dropped to chance levels (36%, p=0.9406, permutation test), likely because of the curse of dimensionality.
evidence: This claim is based on SVM classification results using full connectivity matrices.

claim: Classification based on the proportion of picture trials did not yield significant accuracy with any of the graph metrics.
source: In this control analysis, we did not observe significant classification accuracy with the subnetwork-wise PCs (48%, p=0.6349, permutation test; Figure 8A), with the subnetwork-wise local efficiency (44%, p=0.8713, permutation test; Figure 8B), or with the inter-subnetwork efficiency (44%, p=0.8713, permutation test; Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is based on control analysis results shown in Figure 8.

claim: Classification based on RT did not yield significant accuracy with any of the graph metrics.
source: Again, we did not observe significant classification accuracy with the subnetwork-wise PCs (50%, p=0.5566, permutation test; Figure 8A), with the subnetwork-wise local efficiency (44%, p=0.8000, permutation test; Figure 8B), or with the inter-subnetwork efficiency (38%, p=0.9595, permutation test; Figure 8C).
evidence: This claim is based on control analysis results shown in Figure 8.

claim: The observed differences in functional network architecture were specifically related to encoding performance, not to simple visual stimulation or RT for semantic judgment.
source: Overall, these results suggest that the observed differences in functional network architecture were specifically related to encoding performance, not to simple visual stimulation or RT for semantic judgment.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the control analysis results.

claim: The finding of higher global efficiency during the high encoding state was maintained even for 7.2 s (10 TRs) time windows.
source: Importantly, our finding of higher global efficiency during the high encoding state was maintained even for 7.2 s (10 TRs) time windows.
evidence: This claim is based on robustness checks with different window sizes.

claim: The proportions of reliable edges were significantly high in both high and low encoding states relative to randomized networks.
source: We found that the proportions of reliable edges were significantly high in both high and low encoding states (relative to randomized networks; Supplementary file 1U), and that they were not statistically different from each other (z(24) = 1.2916, p=0.1965; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on edge reliability analysis.

claim: The proportions of reliable edges were not statistically different between the high and low encoding states.
source: We found that the proportions of reliable edges were significantly high in both high and low encoding states (relative to randomized networks; Supplementary file 1U), and that they were not statistically different from each other (z(24) = 1.2916, p=0.1965; Figure 5—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This claim is based on edge reliability analysis.

claim: There was no significant difference in mean FD between the high and low encoding states.
source: We observed no significant difference in mean FD between the high and low encoding states (high: 0.1078 ± 0.0096, low: 0.1093 ± 0.0086; z(24) = −1.9238, p=0.0544), and there were no correlations between the window-wise FD and memory encoding performance (Pearson's r = −0.0742 ± 0.1794; z(24) = −1.8700, p=0.0615), global efficiency (Pearson's r = −0.0429 ± 0.2557; z(24) = −0.9014, p=0.3674), or modularity (Pearson's r = 0.0160 ± 0.1872; z(24) = 0.1211, p=0.9036).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of framewise displacement.

claim: The difference in global efficiency between the high and low encoding states remained significant after regressing out window-wise FD.
source: We found that the difference in global efficiency between the high and low encoding states remained significant after we regressed out window-wise FD from global efficiency (z(24) = 3.9688, p=0.0002).
evidence: This claim is based on analysis controlling for motion confounds.

claim: FC between the hippocampus and occipital cortex was higher during periods of high (vs. low) encoding performance.
source: By analyzing time-varying FC within 36 s time windows, we showed that FC between the hippocampus and occipital cortex, both regarded as SME regions, was higher during periods of high (vs. low) encoding performance.
evidence: This claim is based on FC analysis results.

claim: Successful encoding of visual information is supported by functional interactions between the visual area and the hippocampus.
source: This may indicate that successful encoding of visual information is supported by functional interactions between the visual area and the hippocampus, a key structure for memory formation (Eichenbaum et al., 2007).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FC results, supported by citation.

claim: During the periods of high (vs. low) encoding performance, FC was increased between specific brain regions, whereas it was decreased between another specific set of regions.
source: Importantly, during the periods of high (vs. low) encoding performance, FC was increased between specific brain regions, whereas it was decreased between another specific set of regions (see Supplementary file 1D and 1E for complete lists).
evidence: This claim is based on FC analysis results.

claim: Enhanced long-range interregional FC is important for better encoding performance.
source: Our results indicate that enhanced long-range interregional FC is important for better encoding performance (which was also confirmed by graph analysis).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the FC and graph analysis results.

claim: At the entire-network level, there was a higher degree of integration (as measured by global efficiency) during periods of high encoding performance.
source: At the entire-network level, we found a higher degree of integration (as measured by global efficiency) during periods of high encoding performance.
evidence: This claim is based on graph analysis results.

claim: Greater integration during the high encoding state was observed in the SAN and SUB subnetworks.
source: When we examined individual subnetworks, we observed greater integration during the high encoding state in the SAN and SUB subnetworks.
evidence: This claim is based on subnetwork-wise graph analysis results.

claim: The subcortical nodes may play a unique role in incidental memory encoding, contributing to both within- and across-subnetwork functional interactions and serving as a hub to support large-scale network integration.
source: Therefore, the subcortical nodes (i.e., the thalamus and putamen) may play a unique role in incidental memory encoding, contributing to both within- and across-subnetwork functional interactions and serving as a hub to support large-scale network integration (Bell and Shine, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation of the graph analysis results, supported by citation.

claim: The DMN was the second notable subnetwork showing higher inter-subnetwork integration with many subnetworks during the high encoding state.
source: Following the SUB, the DMN was the second notable subnetwork showing higher inter-subnetwork integration with many subnetworks (i.e., the CON, VIN, FPN, SAN, and SUB) during the high encoding state.
evidence: This claim is based on inter-subnetwork efficiency analysis results.

claim: Inter-subnetwork integration between the DMN and other subnetworks was related to within-individual time-to-time fluctuations of memory performance.
source: Importantly, the current study extends previous findings by revealing that inter-subnetwork integration between the DMN and other subnetworks was related to within-individual time-to-time fluctuations of memory performance, providing further evidence of a central role of the DMN in successful memory encoding.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the study's findings.

claim: The use of graph metrics can efficiently reduce the number of features and achieve more accurate predictions.
source: When we used the entire connectivity patterns as the input, the classification accuracy dropped to chance levels. This suggests that the use of graph metrics can efficiently reduce the number of features and achieve more accurate predictions.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the multivariate classification results.

claim: The finding of large-scale integration associated with encoding performance was above and beyond the effect of motion confounds.
source: Although motion confounds would be expected to influence both momentary encoding performance and dynamic FC patterns, our supplement analyses suggest that the finding of large-scale integration associated with encoding performance was above and beyond the effect of motion confounds.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the motion confound control analyses.

claim: A network can exhibit both high integration and high modularity simultaneously through sparse long-range connections across communities.
source: Importantly, theoretical studies have shown that a network can exhibit both high integration and high modularity simultaneously through sparse long-range connections across communities (Tononi et al., 1994; Watts and Strogatz, 1998; Pan and Sinha, 2009; Meunier et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to theoretical studies.

claim: Integration and segregation are not necessarily incompatible with each other.
source: Recent empirical studies of brain networks have also shown that integration and segregation are not necessarily incompatible with each other (Mohr et al., 2016; Bertolero et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to recent empirical studies.

claim: The results regarding the modularity difference associated with memory encoding performance appeared to be less robust compared with those of global efficiency.
source: However, the results regarding the modularity difference associated with memory encoding performance appeared to be less robust compared with those of global efficiency (i.e., the analysis based on a subset of participants whose FD was less dependent on memory performance).
evidence: This is a statement about the robustness of the modularity findings.

claim: Window-to-window fluctuations in the graph metrics substantially covaried with overall FC strength.
source: Third, our additional analysis controlling for overall FC strength suggested that window-to-window fluctuations in the graph metrics substantially covaried with overall FC strength.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis controlling for overall FC strength.

claim: The findings are not attributable to differential proportions of false-positive edges.
source: Importantly, we examined the reliability of edges across time windows, and confirmed that our findings are not attributable to differential proportions of false-positive edges (Zalesky et al., 2014; van den Heuvel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is based on edge reliability analysis.

claim: Intrinsic, spontaneous dynamics of FC patterns may underlie temporal fluctuations in encoding performance.
source: Given these previous findings, it could be hypothesized that intrinsic, spontaneous dynamics of FC patterns underlie temporal fluctuations in encoding performance.
evidence: This is a hypothesis based on previous findings.

claim: Different levels of encoding performance across the time windows may induce time-varying FC patterns.
source: However, we cannot rule out the possibility that different levels of encoding performance across the time windows induce time-varying FC patterns.
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis about causality.

claim: Large-scale network states with much shorter timescales (e.g., less than a second) may also be related to individual memory-encoding events.
source: Furthermore, given the rapid nature of memory-encoding processes (Viskontas et al., 2006), large-scale network states with much shorter timescales (e.g., less than a second) may also be related to individual memory-encoding events.
evidence: This is a speculation about network states at shorter timescales, supported by citation.

claim: Large-scale neural synchronization with timescales of hundreds of milliseconds across many regions are associated with both successful memory encoding and retrieval.
source: Recent human electrophysiological studies have shown that large-scale neural synchronization with timescales of hundreds of milliseconds across many regions (e.g., MTL, ventral parietal, and prefrontal cortices) are associated with both successful memory encoding and retrieval (Watrous et al., 2013; Solomon et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to electrophysiological studies.

claim: A total of 30 university students participated in the study.
source: A total of 30 university students (20 males; age 18–22 years, mean ± SD = 20.0±1.2) participated in the study after providing written informed consent.
evidence: This is a description of the study participants.

claim: Four participants who fell asleep in the scanner and did not respond in more than 20 trials were excluded from the analysis.
source: Four participants who fell asleep in the scanner and did not respond in more than 20 trials were excluded from the analysis.
evidence: This describes participant exclusion criteria.

claim: The remaining 25 participants were available for the analysis.
source: The remaining 25 participants (17 males; age 18–22 years, mean ± SD = 20.1±1.1) were therefore available for the analysis.
evidence: This describes the final sample size.

claim: All experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of Kochi University of Technology.
source: All experimental procedures were approved by the Ethics Committee of Kochi University of Technology.
evidence: This is a statement about ethical approval.

claim: Stimuli consisted of color pictures and a white fixation cross.
source: Stimuli consisted of color pictures (sized 8° × 6°) and a white fixation cross (sized 0.8° × 0.8°).
evidence: This describes the experimental stimuli.

claim: The pictorial stimuli included 360 pictures showing man-made objects and 360 pictures showing natural objects.
source: The pictorial stimuli included 360 pictures showing man-made objects (e.g. commodities, stationery, musical instruments, and appliances) and 360 pictures showing natural objects (e.g. animals, plants, fruits, and natural scenes).
evidence: This describes the types of pictorial stimuli used.

claim: All color pictures underwent luminance, contrast, and spatial frequency equalizing.
source: All color pictures underwent luminance, contrast, and spatial frequency equalizing by in-house MATLAB (MathWorks, Natick, MA) code (freely available at https://github.com/Ruedeerat/RGBshine/, Keerativittayayut, 2018; copy archived at https://github.com/elifesciences-publications/RGBshine) adapted from the SHINE toolbox (Willenbockel et al., 2010).
evidence: This describes image preprocessing procedures.

claim: Participants studied 360 pictures in three runs during the incidental memory encoding task.
source: In the incidental memory encoding task, participants studied 360 pictures in three runs.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Each run began with a central fixation cross for 15 s.
source: Each run began with a central fixation cross for 15 s, followed by a continuous series of 180 rapidly intermixed trials.
evidence: This describes the experimental procedure.

claim: Sixty man-made picture trials, 60 natural-made picture trials, and 60 fixation trials were pseudo-randomly presented.
source: Sixty man-made picture trials, 60 natural-made picture trials, and 60 fixation trials were pseudo-randomly presented with counterbalancing (each trial type followed every other trial type equally often).
evidence: This describes the trial composition and randomization.

claim: For a picture trial, a pictorial stimulus was presented on the screen for 2500 ms, followed by a 500 ms presentation of a fixation cross.
source: For a picture trial, a pictorial stimulus was presented on the screen for 2500 ms, followed by a 500 ms presentation of a fixation cross.
evidence: This describes the trial timing.

claim: The total time for performing the incidental encoding task was approximately 30 min.
source: The total time for performing the incidental encoding task was approximately 30 min.
evidence: This describes the task duration.

claim: In the surprise memory test, participants were presented with the 360 studied pictures and 360 unstudied pictures.
source: In the surprise memory test, participants were presented with the 360 studied pictures from the incidental memory encoding task, as well as 360 unstudied pictures.
evidence: This describes the memory test procedure.

claim: Functional data were collected using a multiband echo planar imaging (EPI) pulse sequence.
source: Functional data were collected using a multiband echo planar imaging (EPI) pulse sequence (TR = 720 ms; TE = 33 ms; FA = 52°; FOV = 192 mm; matrix = 64 × 64; in-plane resolution = 3 × 3 mm2; slice thickness = 3 mm; slice gap = 0.75 mm; 45 slices; multi-band acceleration factor = 5), which afforded whole-brain coverage (Xu et al., 2013).
evidence: This describes the fMRI acquisition parameters.

claim: The first five volumes of each run were discarded before preprocessing.
source: The first five volumes of each run were discarded before preprocessing.
evidence: This describes a preprocessing step.

claim: The first set of ROIs consisted of 21 ROIs derived from a recent meta-analysis of the SME/SFE.
source: The first set of ROIs was used to investigate FC patterns among well-established memory-related brain regions. Therefore, we used a set of 21 ROIs derived from a recent meta-analysis of the SME/SFE (Kim, 2011).
evidence: This describes the ROI selection for one analysis.

claim: The second set of ROIs consisted of 224 ROIs from the Power atlas.
source: The second set of ROIs was used to investigate FC patterns across a large-scale brain network. We used 224 ROIs consisting of 10 subnetworks from the Power atlas (Power et al., 2011).
evidence: This describes the ROI selection for another analysis.

claim: To identify brain regions showing the SME and SFE, trial-related activation/deactivation analysis was performed using a general linear model (GLM).
source: To identify brain regions showing the SME (i.e., greater activation in HH than Miss trials) and the SFE (i.e., greater activation in Miss than HH trials), we performed trial-related activation/deactivation analysis using a general linear model (GLM).
evidence: This describes the analysis method for identifying SME/SFE regions.

claim: Residual time series data were extracted from each ROI using a voxel-wise GLM.
source: We extracted residual time series data from each ROI using a voxel-wise GLM, in accord with previous research (Cao et al., 2014; Tompary et al., 2015; Shine et al., 2016; Cohen and D'Esposito, 2016).
evidence: This describes the time series extraction method, supported by citations.

claim: Frames with FD >0.2 mm were censored for scrubbing.
source: For scrubbing, frames with FD >0.2 mm were censored (Power et al., 2012; Power et al., 2014; Laumann et al., 2017), and ignored when computing FC.
evidence: This describes the motion scrubbing procedure, supported by citations.

claim: The extracted time series were divided into 36 s (i.e., 50 TRs) time windows, resulting in 45 windows per participant.
source: To do so, we first divided the extracted time series into 36 s (i.e., 50 TRs) time windows, resulting in 45 windows per participant.
evidence: This describes the windowing procedure.

claim: This window size was determined on the basis of recent studies showing dynamic changes in FC in time periods of 30–40 s.
source: This window size was determined on the basis of recent studies showing dynamic changes in FC in time periods of 30–40 s (Braun et al., 2015; Sadaghiani et al., 2015; Wang et al., 2016; Mohr et al., 2016).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the window size choice, supported by citations.

claim: Participant-specific median values were used for classifying windows into high and low encoding states.
source: We used participant-specific median values for the classification, ensuring roughly equal numbers of windows for the high and low encoding states at an individual level.
evidence: This describes the classification method.

claim: Pearson's correlation coefficients of the time series between all pairs of ROIs were computed for each time window.
source: For each time window, we computed Pearson's correlation coefficients of the time series between all pairs of ROIs, which were Fisher Z-transformed to form a connectivity matrix.
evidence: This describes the FC computation method.

claim: Graph analysis was performed to examine integration and segregation of the 224-node network.
source: We performed graph analysis to examine integration and segregation of the 224-node network, using the Brain Connectivity Toolbox (Rubinov and Sporns, 2010; RRID: SCR_004841).
evidence: This describes the graph analysis approach, supported by citation.

claim: An unweighted, undirected graph was constructed from a 224 × 224 connectivity matrix by applying a proportional threshold of connection density = 0.15.
source: To derive graph metrics from the 224-node network, we constructed an unweighted, undirected graph from a 224 × 224 connectivity matrix by applying a proportional threshold of connection density = 0.15.
evidence: This describes the graph construction method.

claim: Global efficiency is a measure of integration.
source: The global efficiency (Eg) is a measure of integration. A network with high Eg is considered topologically integrated.
evidence: This is a definition of a graph metric.

claim: Local efficiency is a measure of segregation.
source: The local efficiency (Eloc) is a measure of segregation.
evidence: This is a definition of a graph metric.

claim: Modularity is a measure of entire network-level segregation indicating how well a network can be partitioned into distinct communities.
source: We also examined modularity, a measure of entire network-level segregation indicating how well a network can be partitioned into distinct communities (Westphal et al., 2017; Wig, 2017).
evidence: This is a definition of a graph metric, supported by citations.

claim: Across-participant binary classification was performed using support vector machine (SVM) with leave-one-out cross validation.
source: For the multivariate analysis based on graph metrics, we performed across-participant binary classification (with leave-one-out cross validation) using a support vector machine (SVM) implemented in LIBSVM (Chang and Lin, 2011; RRID:SCR_010243).
evidence: This describes the multivariate classification method, supported by citation.
